title: Stack & Queue — Concepts, Operations, and Reasoning
subtitle: 62 questions covering LIFO/FIFO mechanics, complexity, why-questions, applications, and implementation variants

questions.question: What does LIFO stand for, and which data structure follows this principle?
options: Last In First Out — Stack
Last In First Out — Queue
Least In First Out — Stack
Last In First Out — Deque
questions.explanation: LIFO means the most recently inserted element is removed first. A stack implements this via push (insert on top) and pop (remove from top). A queue is FIFO, not LIFO. A deque can behave like either but is not solely LIFO.

questions.question: After executing push(1), push(2), push(3), pop(), what is the top element of the stack?
options: The stack is empty
questions.explanation: push(1)→[1], push(2)→[1,2], push(3)→[1,2,3], pop() removes 3 (the top), leaving [1,2]. The top is now 2.

questions.question: Which operation on a stack returns the top element WITHOUT removing it?
options: pop()
push()
peek()
dequeue()
questions.explanation: peek() (also called top() in some implementations) reads the top element without modifying the stack. pop() removes it. push() adds an element. dequeue() is a queue operation.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of push() and pop() on a stack implemented with a dynamic array (amortized)?
options: O(n) for both
O(1) amortized for both
O(log n) for both
O(1) for push, O(n) for pop
questions.explanation: With a dynamic array, occasional resizing costs O(n) but is amortized over n operations, giving O(1) amortized per operation. Both push and pop are O(1) amortized.

questions.question: Why is a stack used for function call management (the call stack)?
options: Because function calls are served in the order they arrive
Because the most recently called function must return before its caller can resume
Because functions with higher priority execute first
Because the call stack needs random access to any frame
questions.explanation: Function calls nest: foo calls bar, bar must return before foo can continue. This last-called-first-returned pattern is exactly LIFO. A queue (FIFO) would return foo before bar, which is incorrect for nested calls. Priority and random access are unrelated to call semantics.

questions.question: Why is a stack the natural data structure for checking balanced parentheses?
options: Because parentheses must be processed in the order they appear
Because the most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed
Because a stack allows random access to any bracket
Because a stack can store more elements than a queue
questions.explanation: When scanning '([{...}])', the innermost bracket opened must close first — a LIFO pattern. Pushing opening brackets and matching against the top on each closing bracket captures this nesting. FIFO would try to close the outermost bracket first, which is wrong.

questions.question: Why does reversing a string or sequence naturally use a stack?
options: Because a stack processes elements in the same order they were inserted
Because pushing all elements then popping them yields reverse order due to LIFO
Because a stack can hold more characters than other structures
Because random access makes reversal faster
questions.explanation: Pushing all elements onto a stack, then popping, retrieves them in reverse insertion order because LIFO inverts the sequence. A queue would yield the original order. Random access is not a stack property.

questions.question: A stack is implemented using a singly linked list with the head as the top. What is the time complexity of push and pop?
options: O(n) and O(1)
O(1) and O(n)
O(1) and O(1)
O(n) and O(n)
questions.explanation: With the head as the top, push inserts at the head (O(1)) and pop removes the head (O(1)). No traversal is needed. If the tail were used as top instead, both would be O(n) for a singly linked list.

questions.question: What happens when pop() is called on an empty stack?
options: It returns null silently
It returns the last element that was pushed
It causes a stack underflow / exception
It returns 0 by default
questions.explanation: Calling pop() on an empty stack is an underflow condition — the operation is undefined. Implementations either throw an exception or return a sentinel error value, but the correct term is stack underflow. Returning null silently hides bugs.

questions.question: In an infix-to-postfix conversion algorithm, why is a stack used to hold operators?
options: To process operators in the order they appear without reordering
To delay outputting operators until operands with lower precedence are seen, respecting precedence via LIFO ordering
To sort operators by precedence before outputting
To store both operands and operators together
questions.explanation: Operators must wait until their right-hand operands are ready and until operators of lower or equal precedence are encountered. The stack's LIFO property ensures that when a lower-precedence operator arrives, all pending higher-precedence operators are popped in the correct reverse order.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of a stack holding n elements?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: A stack stores n elements, so space grows linearly: O(n). O(1) would mean constant memory regardless of n, which is impossible if the elements themselves must be stored.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the state of this stack after: push(5), push(3), push(7), pop(), push(2)?
options: Bottom→[5, 3, 2]←Top
Bottom→[5, 7, 2]←Top
Bottom→[3, 5, 2]←Top
Bottom→[5, 3, 7, 2]←Top
questions.explanation: push(5)→[5], push(3)→[5,3], push(7)→[5,3,7], pop() removes 7→[5,3], push(2)→[5,3,2]. The top is 2, bottom is 5.

questions.question: What does FIFO stand for, and which data structure implements it?
options: First In First Out — Stack
First In First Out — Queue
Fast Input Fast Output — Queue
First In First Out — Priority Queue
questions.explanation: FIFO means the element inserted earliest is dequeued first. A queue is the canonical FIFO structure. A stack is LIFO. A priority queue orders by priority, not arrival time.

questions.question: In a queue, where does enqueue insert and dequeue remove?
options: Enqueue at front, dequeue at rear
Enqueue at rear, dequeue at front
Both operations happen at the rear
Both operations happen at the front
questions.explanation: A queue inserts (enqueues) at the rear and removes (dequeues) from the front, preserving arrival order. Inserting at front or removing from rear would violate FIFO semantics.

questions.question: After enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C), dequeue(), what is the front element?
options: A
B
C
The queue is empty
questions.explanation: Enqueue A, B, C in order. dequeue() removes A (the front). B becomes the new front.

questions.question: Why is a queue used in Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
options: Because BFS explores the deepest node first and stacks are too slow
Because BFS must explore all neighbors at the current level before going deeper, which requires FIFO ordering
Because a queue allows random access to nodes at any level
Because BFS uses recursion, which naturally uses a queue
questions.explanation: BFS visits nodes level by level. When a node is discovered, its neighbors are added to the rear of the queue and will be processed after all nodes at the current level (already in the queue) are done — exactly FIFO. A stack would give DFS behavior, not BFS.

questions.question: Why is a queue the right structure for a printer spooler?
options: Because the most recently submitted job should print first
Because jobs must be printed in the order they were submitted (fairness)
Because print jobs have priorities that must be respected
Because a queue allows canceling any job in O(1)
questions.explanation: A printer spooler is fair: the first job submitted should print first. This is FIFO. A stack (LIFO) would print the most recent job first, starving earlier submissions. Priority queue would only be appropriate if jobs had explicit priorities.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of enqueue and dequeue on a queue implemented with a doubly linked list?
options: O(n) and O(1)
O(1) and O(n)
O(1) and O(1)
O(log n) and O(log n)
questions.explanation: With tail pointer for enqueue and head pointer for dequeue, both operations are O(1) — insert at tail, remove at head, each with direct pointer access.

questions.question: In an array-based queue without circular indexing, what problem arises after many enqueue/dequeue operations?
options: The rear pointer overflows before the array is logically full
The front pointer catches up to the rear pointer, causing underflow
Elements are overwritten by new enqueues
Dequeue becomes O(n) due to shifting
questions.explanation: Each dequeue increments the front pointer, leaving empty slots at the beginning. Eventually the rear pointer reaches the array's physical end even though those freed front slots are available, wasting space. A circular array solves this by wrapping the rear pointer.

questions.question: Why does a circular queue solve the space-waste problem of a linear array queue?
options: Because it doubles the array size when full
Because rear and front pointers wrap around using modulo, reusing freed slots at the front
Because it stores elements in sorted order
Because it uses a linked list internally
questions.explanation: In a circular queue, rear = (rear + 1) % capacity and front = (front + 1) % capacity. This wraps the rear pointer back to index 0 when it reaches the end, reusing the freed slots without shifting elements.

questions.question: How is the 'full' condition detected in a circular queue that wastes one slot?
options: (rear + 1) % capacity == front
rear == front
rear == capacity - 1
front == 0 and rear == capacity - 1
questions.explanation: The common trick is to sacrifice one slot: the queue is full when (rear + 1) % capacity == front. If rear == front were used for both full and empty, the two states would be indistinguishable.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of dequeue on a naive array-based queue (no circular indexing, shifting elements)?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: Without circular indexing, removing from the front requires shifting all remaining n-1 elements one position left, giving O(n). Circular indexing or a linked list avoids this.

questions.question: Which data structure would best model a 'undo/redo' feature in a text editor, and why?
options: Queue — because undo operations are processed in arrival order
Stack — because the most recent action must be undone first (LIFO)
Priority Queue — because actions with higher importance are undone first
Circular Queue — because undo wraps around to the oldest action
questions.explanation: Undo reverses the most recent action, then the second most recent, and so on — classic LIFO. A stack naturally models this. A queue would undo the oldest action first, which is wrong for undo semantics.

questions.question: Which data structure models a 'waiting line at a ticket counter', and why?
options: Stack — because the last person in line is served first
Queue — because the first person in line is served first (fairness)
Priority Queue — because people with tickets are served before others
Deque — because people can join from either end
questions.explanation: A ticket counter serves in arrival order — FIFO. A stack would serve the most recent arrival first, which is unfair. A priority queue applies only when explicit priorities exist.

questions.question: DFS on a graph can be implemented iteratively using which structure?
options: Queue
Stack
Priority Queue
Circular Queue
questions.explanation: Iterative DFS uses a stack: push the start node, then repeatedly pop and push unvisited neighbors. The LIFO property mimics the recursive call stack's behavior, going deep before backtracking. A queue gives BFS.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of stacks needed to implement a queue?
questions.explanation: Two stacks suffice: enqueue pushes onto stack1; dequeue pops from stack2. When stack2 is empty, all of stack1 is poured into stack2 (reversing the order), restoring FIFO. One stack cannot achieve FIFO without additional storage.

questions.question: When implementing a queue using two stacks, what is the amortized time complexity of dequeue?
options: O(n) worst case, O(1) amortized
O(1) always
O(log n) amortized
O(n) always
questions.explanation: A single dequeue can cost O(n) when stack2 is empty and all n elements must be transferred from stack1. But each element is transferred at most once, so over n operations the total cost is O(n), giving O(1) amortized per dequeue.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of queues needed to implement a stack?
questions.explanation: One queue is sufficient: to pop, rotate all but the last element to the rear (dequeue and re-enqueue n-1 times), then dequeue the last element. Two queues also work but one is the minimum.

questions.question: In a 'stack with min' (a stack that supports getMin() in O(1)), why is an auxiliary stack needed?
options: To store all elements in sorted order
To track the minimum at each level so that when the current min is popped, the previous min is immediately available
To allow random access to any element
To reduce the space complexity to O(1)
questions.explanation: After popping the current minimum, the next minimum must be known instantly. An auxiliary stack that mirrors the main stack's minimums at each depth provides this: its top always equals the current minimum, and it pops in sync with the main stack.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of peek() on a stack?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: peek() reads the top element via a direct pointer or index — no traversal needed. It is always O(1) regardless of stack size.

questions.question: Which scenario would cause a stack overflow (not to be confused with underflow)?
options: Calling pop() on an empty stack
Infinite recursion exhausting the call stack's memory
Calling peek() when the stack has one element
Pushing more elements than the queue can hold
questions.explanation: Stack overflow occurs when the stack's memory is exhausted — most commonly by infinite recursion pushing unlimited frames onto the call stack. Underflow is pop() on empty. peek() on a singleton is valid. Queues are separate from stacks.

questions.question: Why is a stack preferred over a queue for evaluating postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) expressions?
options: Because operands must be processed in arrival order
Because when an operator is encountered, the two most recently seen operands must be retrieved immediately
Because the expression must be sorted before evaluation
Because a queue provides faster access to the front element
questions.explanation: In postfix evaluation, operands are pushed; when an operator is seen, the two operands on top (most recently pushed) are popped and combined. This last-in-first-out retrieval is exactly LIFO. A queue would retrieve operands in insertion order, which would not correctly pair them with operators.

questions.question: Given the postfix expression '3 4 + 2 *', what is the result?
questions.explanation: Push 3, push 4. '+' pops 4 and 3, pushes 7. Push 2. '*' pops 2 and 7, pushes 14. Result: 14.

questions.question: A queue is being used to implement a CPU scheduling algorithm where every process gets equal time slices. What scheduling algorithm is this?
options: Shortest Job First
Round Robin
Priority Scheduling
LIFO Scheduling
questions.explanation: Round Robin dequeues a process, runs it for a time slice, then re-enqueues it if it hasn't finished. The FIFO property ensures all processes are treated fairly in circular order.

questions.question: What property distinguishes a deque (double-ended queue) from a standard queue?
options: A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends
A deque stores elements in sorted order
A deque only allows deletion, not insertion
A deque has O(log n) access for all operations
questions.explanation: A deque supports insertFront, insertRear, deleteFront, and deleteRear. A standard queue only allows insertRear and deleteFront. This makes a deque more flexible — it can simulate both stacks and queues.

questions.question: Why does a deque generalize both a stack and a queue?
options: Because it stores elements in sorted order like a priority queue
Because by restricting which ends are used, it can behave as LIFO (stack) or FIFO (queue)
Because it has O(1) access to any element like an array
Because it automatically resizes when full
questions.explanation: If only insertFront and deleteFront are used, behavior is LIFO (stack). If insertRear and deleteFront are used, behavior is FIFO (queue). The deque's two-end access subsumes both restricted patterns.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the 'Sliding Window Maximum' algorithm that uses a deque?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(k*n) where k is window size
questions.explanation: Each element is added to and removed from the deque at most once, giving O(n) total. The deque maintains indices of potentially maximum elements in decreasing order. A naive approach would be O(n*k).

questions.question: How does a priority queue differ from a standard queue?
options: A priority queue removes elements in LIFO order
A priority queue removes the element with the highest (or lowest) priority regardless of insertion order
A priority queue only allows insertion, not deletion
A priority queue uses a stack internally
questions.explanation: In a standard queue, dequeue order equals insertion order (FIFO). In a priority queue, the element with the highest priority (e.g., smallest value in a min-heap) is dequeued first, regardless of when it was inserted.

questions.question: Why is a heap (not a sorted array) typically used to implement a priority queue?
options: Because a heap allows O(1) access to any element
Because a heap provides O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min, whereas a sorted array has O(n) insert
Because a heap uses less memory than any other structure
Because a heap supports FIFO ordering natively
questions.explanation: A sorted array gives O(1) extract-min but O(n) insert (must maintain order). A heap balances both at O(log n), making it efficient for dynamic workloads where insertions and extractions are interleaved.

questions.question: Which statement about a stack's isEmpty() check is correct regarding its time complexity?
options: O(n) because all elements must be counted
O(1) because only the size counter or top pointer needs to be checked
O(log n) because the stack must be partially traversed
O(n) only for linked-list stacks
questions.explanation: isEmpty() checks whether size == 0 or top == null — a single comparison regardless of how many elements are stored. This is O(1) for both array and linked-list implementations.

questions.question: What is the key invariant maintained in a monotonic stack?
options: Elements are stored in sorted order at all times
The stack contains elements in strictly increasing or strictly decreasing order
The top of the stack always holds the maximum element
The stack is never allowed to grow beyond O(log n) elements
questions.explanation: A monotonic stack pops elements that violate a monotone ordering (increasing or decreasing) before pushing a new element. This is useful for problems like 'next greater element'. It is not necessarily sorted across all elements, only among what remains.

questions.question: Why does a monotonic stack solve the 'Next Greater Element' problem in O(n)?
options: Because it sorts all elements before scanning
Because each element is pushed and popped at most once, so total operations are O(n)
Because binary search finds the next greater element in O(log n) per query
Because the stack only holds n/2 elements at any time
questions.explanation: Each of the n elements is pushed onto the monotonic stack exactly once and popped at most once. The total number of push and pop operations is at most 2n, giving O(n) overall rather than O(n^2) for the naive nested-loop approach.

questions.question: In the 'Largest Rectangle in Histogram' problem, why is a stack used?
options: To store bar heights in sorted order
To efficiently find the nearest shorter bar on each side, enabling rectangle area computation
To sort bars by height before computing areas
To store all possible rectangles for later comparison
questions.explanation: A monotonic stack tracks bars in increasing height order. When a shorter bar is encountered, it triggers popping taller bars and computing the maximum width for each popped height using the stack's new top as the left boundary. This avoids O(n^2) brute force.

questions.question: What distinguishes a 'bounded queue' from an 'unbounded queue'?
options: A bounded queue allows dequeue only after it is full
A bounded queue has a fixed maximum capacity and blocks or throws on overflow
A bounded queue processes elements in priority order
A bounded queue uses a stack internally
questions.explanation: A bounded (or blocking) queue has a maximum size. When full, enqueue either blocks (in concurrent contexts) or raises an error. An unbounded queue grows dynamically. Bounded queues are critical in producer-consumer scenarios to prevent memory exhaustion.

questions.question: Why is a queue (not a stack) preferred for implementing a web server's request handler?
options: Because the most recently arrived request is the most urgent
Because fairness requires that earlier requests are handled before later ones
Because a queue allows the server to skip slow requests
Because a stack processes requests faster due to LIFO
questions.explanation: Web servers should respect arrival order to ensure fairness and predictable latency. FIFO (queue) achieves this. LIFO (stack) would mean the most recently arrived request is always handled first, causing starvation for earlier requests under high load.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for a specific element in an unsorted stack?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: A stack provides direct access only to its top element. To find an arbitrary element, all elements must be popped (and typically saved elsewhere), requiring O(n) time. There is no indexed or hashed access.

questions.question: After enqueue(10), enqueue(20), dequeue(), enqueue(30), enqueue(40), dequeue(), what elements remain in the queue (front to rear)?
questions.explanation: enqueue 10→[10], enqueue 20→[10,20], dequeue removes 10→[20], enqueue 30→[20,30], enqueue 40→[20,30,40], dequeue removes 20→[30,40]. Front is 30, rear is 40.

questions.question: Why is a queue used in level-order traversal of a binary tree?
options: Because nodes at deeper levels have higher priority
Because each level's nodes are discovered in order, and their children must be processed after all sibling nodes — FIFO ensures this
Because a queue can store parent-child relationships more efficiently
Because trees have cycles that a queue handles better than a stack
questions.explanation: Level-order visits all nodes at depth d before depth d+1. When a node is dequeued, its children are enqueued at the rear. Because all depth-d nodes were enqueued before depth-(d+1) nodes, FIFO ensures correct level-by-level ordering.

questions.question: What is the correct output order if push(1), push(2), push(3) is followed by pop(), pop(), pop()?
questions.explanation: Push in order 1, 2, 3 puts 3 on top. pop() yields 3, then 2, then 1. LIFO reverses the insertion order.

questions.question: A queue is said to be 'empty' when which condition holds (using front and rear indices in a circular array implementation)?
options: front == rear + 1
rear == front
front == capacity - 1
rear == 0
questions.explanation: In the one-wasted-slot circular array convention, empty is detected by front == rear. Full is (rear + 1) % capacity == front. When front catches up to rear after dequeues, the queue is empty.

questions.question: Which data structure is most appropriate for implementing the 'back button' in a web browser?
options: Queue — to return to pages in visit order
Stack — to return to the most recently visited page first
Priority Queue — to revisit important pages first
Deque — to navigate both forward and backward simultaneously
questions.explanation: The back button should go to the most recently visited page, which is LIFO. A stack of visited URLs allows each 'back' click to pop the latest URL. A deque is used when both back and forward navigation must be supported simultaneously.

questions.question: When using a stack to detect a cycle in a directed graph via DFS, what additional tracking is needed beyond a 'visited' set?
options: A count of each node's in-degree
A 'currently in recursion stack' set to distinguish back edges from cross edges
A sorted list of all nodes
A second stack to hold parent nodes
questions.explanation: A node marked 'visited' may have been fully explored in a prior DFS branch. To detect a cycle, a node in the current recursion path (on the stack) must be distinguished from a node visited in a different branch. The 'rec_stack' set serves this purpose.

questions.question: What is the output of the following stack operations: push(A), push(B), push(C), peek(), pop(), peek()?
options: C, B, B
C, C, B
A, C, B
B, C, A
questions.explanation: After push(A,B,C) the stack top is C. peek() returns C without removing it. pop() removes C. peek() now returns B (new top). Sequence: C, C, B.

questions.question: Why is it inefficient to implement a stack using a queue (single queue)?
options: Because a queue cannot store the same data types as a stack
Because either push or pop requires O(n) rotations to bring the correct element to the front
Because a queue automatically sorts elements, breaking LIFO
Because peek() is not supported on queues
questions.explanation: To simulate LIFO with a queue, push must rotate all existing elements to put the new element at the front (O(n)), or pop must rotate all but one element to bring the last-inserted element to the front (O(n)). Either way, one operation costs O(n).

questions.question: In concurrent programming, why is a lock-free queue preferred over a lock-based queue for high-throughput systems?
options: Because a lock-free queue is always faster for single-threaded programs
Because locking creates contention and blocks threads, while lock-free algorithms allow progress without waiting
Because lock-free queues have lower memory usage
Because lock-free queues are simpler to implement correctly
questions.explanation: In high-throughput multi-threaded systems, lock-based queues serialize access: a thread waiting for a lock is blocked, wasting CPU time. Lock-free algorithms use atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) operations so at least one thread always makes progress, improving throughput under contention.

questions.question: What is the best-case time complexity of pop() on a stack implemented as a singly linked list?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: pop() removes the head node: save head, advance head to head.next, return saved value. This is always O(1) regardless of the list size — best, average, and worst cases all match.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid application of a stack?
options: Evaluating arithmetic expressions
Backtracking in maze-solving algorithms
Managing the order of requests in a network router (FIFO scheduling)
Storing activation records during recursive function calls
questions.explanation: Network routers using FIFO scheduling process packets in arrival order — that is a queue application. Arithmetic expression evaluation, backtracking, and function call management all rely on LIFO behavior, making them stack applications.

questions.question: If a stack supports push, pop, and getMin, all in O(1), what is the space overhead compared to a plain stack?
options: O(1) extra
O(log n) extra
O(n) extra
No overhead
questions.explanation: The auxiliary min-stack can grow to O(n) in the worst case (e.g., elements pushed in decreasing order means every push creates a new minimum recorded in the auxiliary stack). The total space doubles at worst.

questions.question: A queue implemented using two stacks performs k enqueue and k dequeue operations. What is the total number of element movements?
options: k
2k
3k
4k
questions.explanation: Each element is pushed onto stack1 once (1 move) and transferred to stack2 once (1 move), for 2 moves total per element. Over k elements: 2k total movements. Dequeuing from stack2 does not count as an additional transfer once elements are there.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'stack frame' and a 'heap allocation' in the context of memory management?
options: Stack frames are allocated on the heap, while heap allocations use the stack
Stack frames are automatically reclaimed when a function returns (LIFO), while heap allocations persist until explicitly freed
Stack frames hold global variables, heap allocations hold local variables
Stack frames are slower to allocate than heap allocations
questions.explanation: The call stack uses LIFO: when a function returns, its frame is popped automatically. Heap memory is manually managed (or garbage-collected) — it persists beyond the function that allocated it. Stack allocation is faster but size-limited; heap is flexible but requires explicit management.

questions.question: For the problem 'generate all valid combinations of n pairs of parentheses', which structure tracks the recursive state most naturally?
options: Queue — to explore combinations breadth-first
Stack — because backtracking requires undoing choices in reverse order
Priority Queue — to generate combinations in lexicographic order
Circular Queue — to cycle through combinations
questions.explanation: Backtracking explores a choice, recurses deeper, then undoes the choice before trying the next option. This undo-last-choice behavior is LIFO, naturally matching a stack (or the recursive call stack). A queue would not support undoing choices.

questions.question: In a queue of n elements, what is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element from the front without removing any elements?
options: O(k)
O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: A queue only provides direct access to the front. To reach the k-th element, k-1 elements must be dequeued (and re-enqueued to preserve the queue). This takes O(k) time. In the worst case k = n, so O(n).

questions.question: What problem arises if a producer adds to a bounded queue faster than the consumer removes, and the queue is full?
options: The queue automatically doubles in capacity
The producer is blocked or receives an overflow error, potentially causing data loss or deadlock
The consumer skips elements to keep up
The queue converts to LIFO mode
questions.explanation: In a bounded queue used for producer-consumer communication, a full queue blocks the producer (in blocking implementations) or causes enqueue to fail/drop data. If both producer and consumer are waiting on each other, deadlock can occur. This must be handled by backpressure mechanisms.

questions.question: Which of the following operations is NOT supported in O(1) by a standard stack?
options: push
pop
peek
search for an arbitrary element
questions.explanation: push, pop, and peek all operate on the top element and are O(1). Searching for an arbitrary element requires traversing the stack (O(n)) since there is no direct access beyond the top.

questions.question: Why is an array-based stack generally faster in practice than a linked-list stack, even though both have O(1) operations?
options: Because arrays support more operations than linked lists
Because arrays have better cache locality — elements are contiguous in memory, reducing cache misses
Because arrays are easier to implement
Because array-based stacks avoid stack overflow errors
questions.explanation: O(1) describes asymptotic behavior but not constants. Array elements are stored contiguously, so accessing top is cache-friendly. Linked-list nodes may be scattered in memory, causing cache misses on each push/pop. In practice, cache locality often makes arrays 2-5x faster.
